title: This AI Tamagotchi Turns Everyday Objects Into Needy Little Pets
summary:
Your plant is thirsty. You forgot to water it — again. But this time, a tiny screen attached to the pot shows a sad little plant pet, drooping and dejected. Suddenly, grabbing the watering can feels urgent.

That is the idea behind OATs, short for Object Agent Twins: tiny AI avatars on small E Ink screens that pair with everyday objects. Daehwa Kim, a fifth-year PhD student at Carnegie Mellon University, created them. She presented the project at a computing conference in Detroit in early November and earned two Honorable Mention awards.

The idea takes a page from Tamagotchi, the egg-shaped toys from the 1990s that held digital pets needing constant care. Kim wanted to bring that same feeling of caring to real objects. 'We bring this joy of caring from virtual to physical objects,' she said.

Each OAT has a small screen linked to sensors that track moisture, temperature, humidity, light and motion. The main module costs about $20. Through a web portal, you can name your OAT and pick the sensors that fit your object. The screen shows faces made with Google's Gemini image tool, changing with the sensor readings.

The uses are simple and fun. Attach one to a skateboard, and if it sits still for a few days, the avatar looks sad and lonely. Hop on, and it cheers up with happy faces. Attach one to a coffee machine, and it gets excited when the machine grinds beans. Someone even stuck one on a dumbbell to track workouts — exercising meant not disappointing the little pet.

The demo also sparked a debate about giving AI humanlike feelings. Some worry cute, emotional robots could make people trust AI too much. Kim says that is why OATs keep their interactions small — just expressive faces on a tiny screen.
why_it_matters: OATs show how a little emotion can change everyday habits, turning chores into caring, and they raise a real question about how much we should trust machines that act as if they feel.

background_read: A Tamagotchi is a small egg-shaped toy that holds a digital pet, and the owner has to feed it, play with it and care for it, or it gets unhappy.
OATs take that same idea and attach it to real things: a tiny screen and sensors watch how an object is doing, and the little face on the screen shows whether it needs attention.
The point is to turn boring chores, like watering a plant or using a skateboard, into caring for a pet, so people feel like looking after the object.
The project also raises a wider question about AI that acts as if it has feelings, and whether cute, emotional machines could make people trust them too much.
